words: Okay. My name is Michael Kawahara. I graduated from Grinnell 1971. I am from Honolulu, Hawaii and I was born and raised there and I still live there today. I guess one of the questions that has always been posed to me is how did I end up coming to a school in the state of Iowa and a little bit of history. World War II, December 7th Japanese bomb Pearl Harbor. One of the reactions from President Roosevelt at that time was 120,000 Japanese Americans on the West Coast. 70% of them being US citizens are summarily detained and placed into detention facilities for the duration of the war. At the same time, President Roosevelt also authorized an experimental unit of Japanese Americans to be formed in the army, battalion sized approximately 1,100 personnel. All the original members of this battalion, which ultimately became known as the 100th battalion, all of them originally came from Hawaii, one of them being my father.

speaker: Michael
words: Because of the success of the 100th battalion, President Roosevelt subsequently authorized the creation of a regiment of Japanese American soldiers. That's three battalions. This became the 442 regimental combat team, which became in the United States Army history, the most decorated unit in the United States Army history for its size and duration.

speaker: Michael
words: During World War II, the 100th and the 442 fought with 34th infantry battalion in Italy. 34th Infantry Division was known as the Red Bulls. Today it is a National Guard Division centered in Minnesota, but during World War II, it was made up of primarily Iowans. When I grew up, I lived in a subdivision that the original owners had to be veterans of World War II, the Korean War. And so all my neighbors, my judo instructors, my little league coaches, all of them were in the 442 or the hundredth. And one of the things that I remember from an early age that I'm talking about was their comrade in arms of the 34th division, namely all Iowans. And so unlike a lot of people in Hawaii, I knew about the state of Iowa from the time I was about eight, nine years old. And so when it came time to apply for colleges, one of the places recommended to me was a Grinnell.

speaker: Michael
words: And because it was an Iowa, I had a historic, shall we say, affiliation. So when I was accepted here, there was no question I would be happy to come here. And that's how I ended up at Grinnell. But I'm sorry, there's a little bit of history involved in that.

words: And while I was at Grinnell here, these are an acronyms because these are all part of history that probably no one like yourself or anyone who graduated later. I was a federal prosecutor and I prosecuted organized crime racketeering, drug trafficking, money laundering kinds of cases. I also stayed in the Air Force Reserve and I retired as a full colonel. words: Memories from campus. A lot of them are old time memories because at that time north campus was all men. South campus was all women. speaker: Michael

speaker: Michael
words: I am now on active duty with the Air Force. I'm stationed in Texas and I was returning back to base, either I was traveling because Texas is such a historical place. speaker: Michael
words: I'm a Japanese American, but I'm an American citizen. And he said, "No, no, no, no, no. You know anybody in that Jap regiment." Now my father at this point had, because of his language ability, he was not involved in Southern France with the 36th division, but he had already gone into the military intelligence service because of his language ability. So he was nowhere near there when the rescue of the Texas battalion occurred, but this was not the time to tell the truth. So using my lawyerly skills, I lied through my teeth and said, "Yes, my father was there, Voge Mountains for the 36th division." speaker: Michael
words: And to this day, I couldn't understand whether he was one of those who was rescued or saved or it was his sibling or it was a friend or whatnot. In any event, I ended up with a free tank of gas.

words: And as I left, I remember when I got home, I made a long distance call to my friend, no internet, no ... They had to give me long distance call through the operator, right? speaker: Michael
words: But I'll tell you, when he called me a jab, I said, "This is going to go bad." All I could think about was how I could get to my firearm if necessary.
